name: Mentalis muscle resuspension

card.summary: Surgical step of reattaching the chin muscle after genioplasty or implant placement so the chin keeps its natural contour.
card.note: Part of surgery; outcomes depend on surgeon technique.

quick.overview:
The mentalis is the paired chin muscle that lifts the lower lip and dimples the chin skin. During chin surgery such as T-osteotomy genioplasty, it must be carefully reattached, a step called mentalis resuspension or repair.

The aim is a natural-looking chin and lower lip after the bone or implant has changed the contour.
quick.how: Done by the surgeon as part of genioplasty or implant surgery, closing the muscle layer over the reshaped chin. Patients do not perform it themselves.
quick.risks: Genioplasty complications include swelling, hematoma, temporary lip weakness or numbness, infection and nerve damage; surgeon experience reduces risk.

lead: Mentalis muscle resuspension is the surgical reattachment of the mentalis, the muscle at the tip of the chin, after it has been lifted off the bone during genioplasty or chin implant surgery.[1]

The mentalis raises the lower lip and wrinkles or dimples the chin skin.[2] Reattaching it is described as necessary after T-osteotomy, the Korean-developed intraoral technique that narrows and lengthens the chin.[1]
It helps looks by supporting a natural chin soft-tissue shape alongside the bony or implant change.[1]

angle.text: Resuspending the mentalis is a surgeon-performed step that helps the soft tissue sit correctly over the new chin shape.

paras: The mentalis originates near the midline of the mandible and inserts into chin skin and soft tissue; it is supplied by the mandibular branch of the facial nerve.[2]
Chin augmentation includes implants, sliding genioplasty and T-osteotomy, usually 2 to 3 mm of change for the latter. The mentalis must be carefully reattached after T-osteotomy.[1]
Common genioplasty complications are swelling, hematoma and temporary lip weakness or numbness; infection, implant displacement and nerve damage are less common.[1]
